_comment: Heresies levels 16-19: contemporary errors, precise conciliar terminology, live apologetics, capstone

questions.prompt: "If you have enough faith, God will make you materially wealthy and physically healthy -- suffering only happens to those whose faith is deficient" is answered directly by which scriptural teaching?
choices: "No one can serve two masters... You cannot serve God and mammon" (Matthew 6:24), read alongside Christ's own teaching that his followers must take up their cross, not escape it
The parable of the wedding feast
The genealogy of Christ in Matthew's Gospel
The instruction to render to Caesar what is Caesar's
questions.correctAnswer: "No one can serve two masters... You cannot serve God and mammon" (Matthew 6:24), read alongside Christ's own teaching that his followers must take up their cross, not escape it
questions.explanation: The prosperity gospel inverts the New Testament's own witness -- Christ was not materially wealthy, promised his followers persecution rather than ease, and explicitly warned against treating wealth as a sign of divine favor to be pursued as an end. This level opens this topic's own turn from a chronological survey to errors still actively circulating today.
questions.hint: Look for the verse that names wealth itself as a rival master to God, not a reward for enough faith.

questions.prompt: True or False: The prosperity gospel is best understood as a genuinely new invention of the modern era, with no real precedent among any error this topic has already covered.
questions.explanation: False. In real substance, it shares Pelagianism's own old confidence that human effort -- here, generating enough faith -- can secure what only grace freely gives, dressed in modern language about wealth and health rather than ancient language about merit.
questions.hint: Recall Pelagianism, several levels back in this topic, and consider whether this level's error shares its underlying confidence in human effort.

questions.prompt: A popular spirituality that blends Christian language with horoscopes, crystals, and channeling "universal energy," while insisting it's all compatible with being Catholic, runs into which Catechism teaching most directly?
choices: Its condemnation of divination and the occult -- horoscopes, astrology, and consulting other hidden powers over one's future or fortune -- as contrary to the honor and trust owed to God alone
Its teaching on the just war doctrine
Its teaching on the canon of Scripture
Its teaching on liturgical vestment colors
questions.correctAnswer: Its condemnation of divination and the occult -- horoscopes, astrology, and consulting other hidden powers over one's future or fortune -- as contrary to the honor and trust owed to God alone
questions.explanation: This kind of syncretism rarely presents itself as a rival religion -- it presents itself as harmless add-ons to an existing faith. The Catechism's section on the first commandment addresses exactly this pattern, naming astrology, palm reading, and recourse to mediums as offenses against the honor and trust owed to God alone.
questions.hint: This teaching is under the first commandment, on what's owed to God alone.

questions.prompt: True or False: Religious syncretism, as this level addresses it, is a genuinely different error from the religious relativism this topic's previous chronological level covered.
questions.explanation: True. Relativism treats every religion's own claims as equally valid alongside one another; syncretism blends fragments of several traditions into one private mixture claimed as fully compatible with any of them -- two genuinely different ways of relativizing Christ's own unique role.
questions.hint: Consider whether treating religions as equally valid options and blending fragments of them together are exactly the same move.

questions.prompt: "Since God is merciful, we can be certain that literally everyone, including the unrepentant, ends up saved in the end" is a real and recurring error. How does the Catechism actually respond to it?
choices: It affirms that the Church can and does hope and pray for the salvation of all, while also teaching that Scripture's warnings about a real possibility of hell must be taken seriously and not presumed away -- hope is not the same as a guarantee
It affirms with certainty that some specific named individuals are in hell
It denies that hell exists at all
It teaches that only baptized Catholics can possibly be saved
questions.correctAnswer: It affirms that the Church can and does hope and pray for the salvation of all, while also teaching that Scripture's warnings about a real possibility of hell must be taken seriously and not presumed away -- hope is not the same as a guarantee
questions.explanation: This is a precise, easily-missed distinction: the Church has never taught that anyone in particular is certainly in hell, and she can rightly hope and pray for the salvation of all -- but turning that hope into a flat guarantee presumes on a mercy Scripture itself warns must not be presumed on.
questions.hint: There's a real difference between hoping and praying for something, and treating it as already guaranteed.

questions.prompt: True or False: Presumption, in the sense this level covers, moves in the same direction as Feeneyism, a much earlier level's own error.
questions.explanation: False, and the contrast is worth naming precisely -- Feeneyism narrowed salvation's real reach too far; presumption widens it into an unwarranted certainty that repentance carries no real stakes, a genuinely opposite distortion of the same real mystery.
questions.hint: Recall Feeneyism from an earlier level, and consider whether it narrowed or widened salvation's own real reach.

questions.prompt: Match each contemporary error to the real teaching that answers it.

pairs.left: Prosperity gospel
pairs.right: Christ's own warning that no one can serve both God and wealth

pairs.left: Religious syncretism
pairs.right: The Catechism's condemnation of divination and the occult under the first commandment

pairs.left: Presumption on God's mercy
pairs.right: Real hope for all, held together with Scripture's real warnings about hell

pairs.left: "Spiritual worldliness," per Evangelii Gaudium
pairs.right: Seeking human glory and comfort rather than God's glory, the Gospel's demands quietly dropped

questions.explanation: These four present-day errors share a real pattern -- each keeps comfortable, religious-sounding language while quietly dropping a real, costly demand of the actual Gospel underneath it.
questions.hint: Each row pairs a live contemporary error with the specific, precise teaching that corrects it.

questions.prompt: Pope Francis's Evangelii Gaudium names a temptation it calls "spiritual worldliness" -- reducing the Gospel to a purely therapeutic, feel-good message with no real demand for conversion. What does the document say this ultimately seeks?
choices: Human glory and personal well-being rather than the glory of God -- a Christianity emptied of the cross, repentance, and the call to holiness, however religious its language sounds
The abolition of the sacraments entirely
A return to a purely ritualistic, works-based religion with no interior conversion at all
The replacement of Scripture with purely private revelations
questions.correctAnswer: Human glory and personal well-being rather than the glory of God -- a Christianity emptied of the cross, repentance, and the call to holiness, however religious its language sounds
questions.explanation: This is the same error the prosperity gospel showed in a cruder form at the start of this level: comforting language kept, the actual demand of the Gospel -- repentance, the cross, real conversion of life -- quietly dropped.
questions.hint: The document is naming what's left when the comforting parts of the Gospel stay but the demanding parts quietly disappear.

questions.prompt: True or False: All four errors this level covers -- prosperity gospel, syncretism, presumption, and spiritual worldliness -- share the same real underlying move, keeping religious language while quietly dropping something the real Gospel actually demands.
questions.explanation: True, and naming this shared pattern is this level's own real point -- these are not four unrelated modern curiosities, but four live variations on one real temptation still active in the Church's own present-day life.
questions.hint: Consider what each of this level's four errors keeps, and what each one quietly drops.

questions.prompt: Having traced this topic's errors from the earliest centuries through today's live temptations, what does the next level in this topic turn to?
choices: This topic's own precise conciliar terminology, now gathered and tested directly
A complete repeat of this same level's material about contemporary errors
A jump backward to the ancient Christological heresies, already fully covered several levels earlier
A subject entirely unrelated to any error this topic has covered so far
questions.correctAnswer: This topic's own precise conciliar terminology, now gathered and tested directly
questions.explanation: The next level shifts from following errors in the order they arose or arise to testing this topic's own precise vocabulary directly -- the exact conciliar terms that have carried the real weight of correction throughout this whole survey.
questions.hint: This is exactly what the next level in this topic covers.

citations.quote: To be acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation... concurring in one Person and one Subsistence.

questions.prompt: Arius taught the Son was a supreme creature, not eternally divine like the Father. Nicaea I's precise rejection used the word 'homoousios' (same substance) rather than a softer term. Why was this specific word necessary to actually condemn Arianism, rather than just asserting 'the Son is divine'?
choices: Because 'homoousios' explicitly rules out any reading of the Son as merely similar to or resembling the Father's nature, closing the exact loophole Arius's own followers could otherwise exploit
Because 'homoousios' was the only Greek word available for the concept
Because the term applies only to the Holy Spirit, not the Son
Because Arius himself proposed and approved the word 'homoousios'
questions.correctAnswer: Because 'homoousios' explicitly rules out any reading of the Son as merely similar to or resembling the Father's nature, closing the exact loophole Arius's own followers could otherwise exploit
questions.explanation: A vaguer assertion like 'the Son is divine' could still be read in an Arian-compatible way (a lesser, derivative kind of divinity). 'Homoousios' -- same substance -- closes that exact loophole by insisting on identity of nature, not mere resemblance, which is precisely why the single precise word did work a general assertion could not.
questions.hint: The problem with a vaguer statement is that it leaves room for exactly the reading Arius wanted.

citations.quote: God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father.

questions.prompt: Chalcedon's four adverbs -- asynchytos, atreptos, adiairetos, achoristos -- work as a single, simultaneous rejection of two different heresies. Which two, and how?
choices: Eutyches's Monophysitism (blending the natures into one), excluded by 'without confusion, without change'; and Nestorius's error (dividing Christ into two subjects), excluded by 'without division, without separation'
Arianism and Pelagianism, neither of which concerns Christ's two natures
Donatism and Albigensianism, both of which concern sacramental validity rather than Christology
Only one heresy, Nestorianism, with the other two adverbs serving no doctrinal purpose
questions.correctAnswer: Eutyches's Monophysitism (blending the natures into one), excluded by 'without confusion, without change'; and Nestorius's error (dividing Christ into two subjects), excluded by 'without division, without separation'
questions.explanation: Chalcedon's genius is answering two opposite errors with one formula: the first pair of adverbs excludes Eutyches's blending of Christ's two natures into a single new nature, while the second pair excludes Nestorius's splitting of Christ into two separate persons or subjects -- a single, carefully worded definition doing double duty.
questions.hint: This is the same four-adverb structure covered in this app's Councils topic -- two pairs, two opposite errors.

citations.quote: To be acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation... concurring in one Person and one Subsistence.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Second Council of Orange (529), in its canons on grace, specifically ruled out the semi-Pelagian claim that a person's own unaided natural effort could supply the very 'beginning of faith,' with grace only assisting afterward.
questions.explanation: Orange II's canons condemn exactly this semi-Pelagian sequencing error -- treating the initial turning toward faith as something natural human effort supplies on its own, with grace arriving only as a later reward or assistance -- insisting instead that grace must move the will even at faith's very first stirring.
questions.hint: This is the same sequencing error the semi-Pelagian controversy always comes back to -- who or what moves first.

citations.quote: if anyone says that this belongs to us by nature and not by a gift of grace... it is proof that he is opposed to the teaching of the Apostles.

questions.prompt: Trent's Decree on Justification, Canon 9, anathematizes the claim that the sinner is justified 'by faith alone' in a specific, precise sense. What does this canon actually target, and what does it NOT target?
choices: It targets the claim that nothing at all, including grace-enabled cooperation, is required for justification beyond bare faith -- it does not target the claim that faith is the necessary beginning and foundation of justification
It targets the entire concept of faith as having any role whatsoever in justification
It targets only Eastern Orthodox theology, not Reformation theology
It has since been formally retracted by a later council
questions.correctAnswer: It targets the claim that nothing at all, including grace-enabled cooperation, is required for justification beyond bare faith -- it does not target the claim that faith is the necessary beginning and foundation of justification
questions.explanation: Canon 9's anathema is precisely targeted: it excludes the claim that justification requires nothing else at all -- no grace-enabled cooperation, no sacramental life, nothing -- beyond bare faith. It does not deny that faith is the necessary root and foundation without which no one can be justified, a point Trent affirms elsewhere in the same decree.
questions.hint: The canon's target is a specific claim about what ELSE is or isn't needed beyond faith, not a denial that faith matters at all.

citations.reference: Council of Trent, Decree on Justification, Canon 9
citations.quote: If any one saith, that by faith alone the impious is justified; in such wise as to mean, that nothing else is required to co-operate in order to the obtaining the grace of Justification, and that it is not in any way necessary, that he be prepared and disposed by the movement of his own will; let him be anathema.

questions.prompt: Donatism held that a sacrament's validity depended on the moral worthiness of the minister administering it. How does the Church's teaching of 'ex opere operato' resolve this?
choices: A sacrament's efficacy depends on Christ's own action working through the rite itself when it is validly performed, not on the personal holiness of the minister, since Christ, not the minister's worthiness, is the true agent of grace in the sacrament
The Church agrees with Donatism that an unworthy minister's sacraments are always invalid
Ex opere operato means the recipient's faith alone determines validity, with the minister playing no role at all
Ex opere operato was formally condemned as heretical alongside Donatism
questions.correctAnswer: A sacrament's efficacy depends on Christ's own action working through the rite itself when it is validly performed, not on the personal holiness of the minister, since Christ, not the minister's worthiness, is the true agent of grace in the sacrament
questions.explanation: 'Ex opere operato' ('from the work worked') teaches that a validly performed sacrament's efficacy comes from Christ's own action through the rite itself, not from the minister's personal holiness -- directly resolving Donatism's error, since a believer receiving a sacrament from a genuinely unworthy but validly ordained minister still receives real grace, Christ himself being the true agent.
questions.hint: The key move is identifying who the real agent of grace in a sacrament actually is -- not the minister's personal holiness.

citations.quote: the sacraments act ex opere operato (literally: by the very fact of the action's being performed), i.e., by virtue of the saving work of Christ, accomplished once for all.

questions.prompt: Match each heresy or claim to the precise conciliar text that answers it.

pairs.left: Arianism (the Son as a lesser, created being)
pairs.right: Nicaea I's homoousios

pairs.left: Eutyches's and Nestorius's opposite christological errors
pairs.right: Chalcedon's four adverbs

pairs.left: Semi-Pelagianism (unaided natural effort as faith's beginning)
pairs.right: Second Council of Orange's canons on grace

pairs.left: Calvin's double predestination
pairs.right: Trent's Decree on Justification and its canons on predestination and grace

questions.explanation: Each of these heresies is answered by a precise, findable conciliar text, not a general appeal to 'Church teaching' -- pinpoint citation is this level's whole discipline.
questions.hint: Every right answer names an actual named council or decree, not a vague reference.

citations.reference: Council of Trent, Decree on Justification

questions.prompt: Nicaea II's answer to iconoclasm turns on a distinction the Greek makes more sharply than English: 'proskynesis' offered to images versus 'latria' reserved to God. Why was having two words essential rather than merely convenient?
choices: Because with one word covering both, any honour paid an image is automatically describable as the worship owed to God alone -- the iconoclast case depends on that collapse
Because Greek was the liturgical language of the East
Because the distinction applies only to images of Christ
Because it allowed images while forbidding statues
questions.correctAnswer: Because with one word covering both, any honour paid an image is automatically describable as the worship owed to God alone -- the iconoclast case depends on that collapse
questions.explanation: The iconoclast argument is only valid if honouring and adoring are the same act. Two words let the Church say what is actually happening: honour passes through the image to its prototype, while adoration terminates in God alone.
questions.hint: Ask what the objection requires in order to work, then notice which word does that work.

questions.prompt: Orange II condemned semi-Pelagianism specifically over sequencing. What exactly did it settle?
choices: That even the beginning of faith and the first desire for it are themselves the work of grace, not a human initiative grace then rewards
That grace is unnecessary for the beginning of faith
That human freedom plays no part in salvation at all
That grace is given only after baptism
questions.correctAnswer: That even the beginning of faith and the first desire for it are themselves the work of grace, not a human initiative grace then rewards
questions.explanation: Semi-Pelagianism conceded that grace was needed for everything after the first step, and kept the first step for man. Orange II moved grace to the very beginning. What it did not settle is the inner mechanics of how grace and freedom meet -- that remained open.
questions.hint: The dispute was about who moves first, not about whether grace is needed at all.

questions.prompt: True or False: Chalcedon's 'without confusion, without change' is aimed at Monophysitism, while 'without division, without separation' is aimed at Nestorianism.
questions.explanation: True. The four adverbs are two pairs answering opposite errors in one breath: the first pair stops the natures being blended, the second stops them being pulled into two subjects. Either error alone could be answered with half the formula; both together require all four.
questions.hint: Two of the adverbs guard against mixing, two against splitting.

questions.prompt: Match each precise conciliar term to the error it was coined or deployed against.

pairs.left: Homoousios
pairs.right: Arian subordination of the Son

pairs.left: Theotokos
pairs.right: Nestorian division of Christ into two subjects

pairs.left: Two natural wills
pairs.right: Monothelite denial of a human will in Christ

pairs.left: Transubstantiation
pairs.right: Denial that the substance becomes Christ's Body and Blood

questions.explanation: Each term is a fence, not an explanation. None of them makes the mystery comprehensible; each rules out one specific misreading, which is why the precise word matters more than a general affirmation would.
questions.hint: Each was chosen because a vaguer word had already been shown to leave a loophole.

questions.prompt: A worship song includes the line, 'Before the Father sent the Son, the Son was not yet there to come.' What historical heresy category does this line most closely recommit?
choices: Arian subordinationism -- treating the Son as not eternally existing alongside the Father, but coming into being at a point before which he did not exist
Docetism -- denying Christ had a real physical body
Donatism -- making sacramental validity depend on the minister's worthiness
Iconoclasm -- rejecting the veneration of sacred images
questions.correctAnswer: Arian subordinationism -- treating the Son as not eternally existing alongside the Father, but coming into being at a point before which he did not exist
questions.explanation: The line's claim -- that there was a 'before' during which the Son 'was not yet there' -- restates the core Arian claim that 'there was a time when he was not,' precisely the subordinationist position Nicaea's homoousios was defined to exclude, regardless of whether the songwriter intended any heresy at all.
questions.hint: The key phrase to notice is a claimed 'before' during which the Son did not yet exist.

citations.quote: God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father.

questions.prompt: A popular self-help framing states: 'God helps those who help themselves -- once you've made the first move on your own, grace finishes the job.' Which historical error category does this most closely recommit?
choices: Semi-Pelagianism -- treating unaided human effort as the necessary first move, with grace arriving only afterward to complete what the person already initiated
Docetism -- denying Christ's true humanity
Monophysitism -- blending Christ's two natures into one
Iconoclasm -- rejecting sacred images
questions.correctAnswer: Semi-Pelagianism -- treating unaided human effort as the necessary first move, with grace arriving only afterward to complete what the person already initiated
questions.explanation: This framing places the 'first move' in unaided human effort, with grace only finishing what a person has already begun on their own -- precisely the sequencing error Orange II's canons on grace (level 6) were built to exclude, distinct from full Pelagianism (which denies grace is needed at all) or a genuinely orthodox account of synergy (where grace itself enables even the first movement toward God).
questions.hint: Look back to level 6 -- this is the same sequencing error Orange II's canons addressed, not full Pelagianism itself.

citations.quote: if anyone says that this belongs to us by nature and not by a gift of grace... it is proof that he is opposed to the teaching of the Apostles.

questions.prompt: An online apologist claims, 'Trent condemned faith alone, full stop -- meaning Catholics teach faith plays no real role in justification.' Using level 6's precise reading of Canon 9, what is the actual disputed point this claim misses?
choices: The canon targets the claim that nothing beyond bare faith is needed for justification, not the claim that faith is a necessary foundation -- the actual dispute concerns what else, if anything, has a real role, not whether faith matters at all
Trent's canon and this claim are in complete agreement with no distortion whatsoever
Trent never actually addressed justification in any of its documents
The canon was written to condemn Catholic teaching on justification, not Reformation teaching
questions.correctAnswer: The canon targets the claim that nothing beyond bare faith is needed for justification, not the claim that faith is a necessary foundation -- the actual dispute concerns what else, if anything, has a real role, not whether faith matters at all
questions.explanation: This restates the caricature level 6 already corrected: Trent's actual target is the claim that nothing else -- no grace-enabled cooperation -- has any role beyond bare faith, not a denial that faith matters. The apologist's summary flattens a precise, narrow disputed point into a much broader and less accurate claim.
questions.hint: Canon 9 targets the claim that NOTHING beyond bare faith is needed -- it does not deny that faith itself matters.

citations.reference: Council of Trent, Decree on Justification, Canon 9
citations.quote: If any one saith, that by faith alone the impious is justified; in such wise as to mean, that nothing else is required to co-operate in order to the obtaining the grace of Justification, and that it is not in any way necessary, that he be prepared and disposed by the movement of his own will; let him be anathema.

questions.prompt: A claim states: 'Christ only seemed to suffer on the cross, since as God he cannot truly experience pain or death.' Which historical heresy category does this most precisely recommit, and why is it a different error than Monophysitism?
choices: Docetism -- denying the reality of Christ's human experience and suffering altogether, which is a different error than Monophysitism's blending of the two natures into one nature
Monophysitism, since both errors concern Christ's divinity
Nestorianism, since both errors concern two subjects in Christ
Arianism, since both errors concern the Son's origin
questions.correctAnswer: Docetism -- denying the reality of Christ's human experience and suffering altogether, which is a different error than Monophysitism's blending of the two natures into one nature
questions.explanation: This claim denies the reality of Christ's human suffering altogether ('only seemed'), which is Docetism's specific error -- distinct from Monophysitism, which grants Christ one real (blended) nature but errs on how the two natures relate, not on whether his suffering was real at all. Precisely identifying which error is at work, rather than lumping every christological error together, is the point of this level.
questions.hint: Docetism denies the reality of the experience itself; Monophysitism is about how the two natures relate, not whether the experience was real.

citations.quote: To be acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation... concurring in one Person and one Subsistence.

questions.prompt: A modern teaching claims Christ's human will was entirely absorbed into and indistinguishable from his divine will, such that he had no genuine human faculty of choice at all. Which historical error category does this most closely resemble?
choices: A monothelite-flavored error -- denying Christ possessed a genuine, distinct human will alongside his divine will
Donatism, since both concern the validity of a minister's actions
Pelagianism, since both concern human free will in salvation generally
Iconoclasm, since both concern how Christ is represented
questions.correctAnswer: A monothelite-flavored error -- denying Christ possessed a genuine, distinct human will alongside his divine will
questions.explanation: Monothelitism specifically denied Christ had a genuine human will distinct from his divine will, teaching instead a single divine will alone -- a claim that Christ's human will was fully 'absorbed' with no real human faculty of choice recreates this same error, distinct from Pelagianism's unrelated question about grace and human free will in salvation.
questions.hint: This error is specifically about how many wills Christ has, not about grace and human freedom in salvation generally.

citations.quote: two natural volitions or wills in him and two natural principles of action which undergo no division, no change, no partition, no confusion... his human will following, and not resisting or struggling, rather in fact subject to his divine and all powerful will.

questions.prompt: Match each modern claim or scenario to the historical error category it recommits.

pairs.left: 'Before the Father sent the Son, the Son was not yet there to come'
pairs.right: Arian subordinationism

pairs.left: 'God helps those who help themselves, then grace finishes the job'
pairs.right: Semi-Pelagianism

pairs.left: 'Christ only seemed to suffer, since as God he cannot truly experience pain'
pairs.right: Docetism

pairs.left: 'Christ's human will was entirely absorbed into his divine will, with no real human choice'
pairs.right: A monothelite-flavored error

questions.explanation: None of these four scenarios names its heresy out loud -- the whole task of this level is recognizing the underlying, precisely named error beneath an unlabeled modern-sounding claim, using the same conciliar distinctions fixed at level 6.
questions.hint: Each right answer is a technical term from level 6, applied here to a scenario that never uses that term itself.

citations.quote: the honour paid to an image traverses it, reaching the model, and he who venerates the image, venerates the person represented in that image.

questions.prompt: A well-meaning post says: 'All religions are just different paths up the same mountain -- the summit is the same.' Which error is this closest to, and why?
choices: Religious relativism -- it makes Christ one route among several rather than the unique mediator
Modalism -- it confuses the Persons of the Trinity
Donatism -- it ties validity to the minister's worthiness
Docetism -- it denies Christ's real humanity
questions.correctAnswer: Religious relativism -- it makes Christ one route among several rather than the unique mediator
questions.explanation: The image is generous in intent and specific in what it denies. If every path arrives, the Incarnation is a local preference rather than the way God actually saved the world. The Church holds both that Christ is the unique mediator and that his grace can reach those who never visibly joined the Church -- which the mountain image cannot express.
questions.hint: Ask what the metaphor implies about whether Christ was necessary.

questions.prompt: A documentary claims: 'Jesus was just a wise teacher until the Council of Nicaea voted him divine in 325.' What is wrong with this, historically and doctrinally?
choices: Nicaea defined language for a divinity already confessed and disputed; it settled how to state it, not whether to invent it
Nicaea did not discuss Christ's divinity at all
The claim is accurate but incomplete
Nicaea rejected Christ's divinity and a later council reversed it
questions.correctAnswer: Nicaea defined language for a divinity already confessed and disputed; it settled how to state it, not whether to invent it
questions.explanation: The dispute Nicaea addressed only makes sense because the Son's divinity was already being confessed and already being contested. A council convenes over a live controversy; there would have been nothing to argue about had the claim been introduced there.
questions.hint: Consider what Arius was arguing against, and when.

questions.prompt: A spiritual writer teaches that the body is a prison the soul escapes at death, and that holiness means despising the physical. Which ancient error is being recommitted?
choices: Gnostic dualism -- treating matter as evil rather than as created good
Pelagianism -- overestimating unaided human effort
Nestorianism -- dividing Christ into two subjects
Iconoclasm -- rejecting the veneration of images
questions.correctAnswer: Gnostic dualism -- treating matter as evil rather than as created good
questions.explanation: Scripture's verdict on creation is that God saw everything he had made and found it very good. Christian asceticism disciplines the body precisely because it is good and destined for resurrection, not because it is a prison to be escaped.
questions.hint: Ask what the Church confesses about the body at the very end of the Creed.

questions.prompt: Match each contemporary statement to the historical error it repeats.

pairs.left: 'The Father, Son and Spirit are three hats God wears'
pairs.right: Modalism

pairs.left: 'A priest in mortal sin cannot confect a valid Eucharist'
pairs.right: Donatism

pairs.left: 'Take the first step toward God and grace will meet you'
pairs.right: Semi-Pelagianism

pairs.left: 'Christ could not really have been afraid in Gethsemane'
pairs.right: A denial of Christ's complete human nature

questions.explanation: None of these announce themselves as heresy, and most are said devoutly. That is the point of this level: errors survive by being restated in language that sounds pious, and recognising the shape matters more than knowing the historical label.
questions.hint: Each is a modern phrasing of something a council already answered.

questions.prompt: Looking back across this whole topic -- from Simon Magus to religious relativism -- what single real pattern connects nearly every error it has covered?
choices: Each takes something real and true and pushes it out of balance, either narrowing it too far or dissolving it into something else entirely
Each error is, in fact, a completely unrelated invention with no connection to any other error in this topic
None of these errors touched anything the Church actually teaches
Every error this topic covers was invented for purely political reasons, with no real theological content
questions.correctAnswer: Each takes something real and true and pushes it out of balance, either narrowing it too far or dissolving it into something else entirely
questions.explanation: This is the real thread running through this whole topic -- Arianism narrowed Christ's divinity, Monophysitism dissolved his humanity, Pelagianism narrowed grace's necessity, Jansenism narrowed its freedom, relativism dissolved Christ's uniqueness. Almost every real heresy is a truth taken out of its proper balance, not a truth invented from nothing.
questions.hint: Consider whether these errors tend to deny something real outright, or distort something real by pushing it too far in one direction.

citations.quote: The Son of God is 'begotten, not made, of the same substance (homoousios) as the Father.'

questions.prompt: True or False: This topic's own real relationship to the Councils topic is best described as the same history told from the opposite side -- the error's own logic here, the council's settled answer there.
questions.explanation: True, and this is worth naming directly at this topic's own close -- Councils traces the Church's settled answers in their own right; Heresies traces the specific errors that made each answer necessary in the first place. Neither topic simply repeats the other.
questions.hint: Recall how this topic's own opening levels described its relationship to the Councils topic.
